categories.name: Chinese Foundation Models
categories.blurb:
Chinese foundation models are large language models built by China's major tech companies and AI labs, including Doubao and Seed from ByteDance, ERNIE from Baidu, GLM from Zhipu AI (also branded Z.AI), Hunyuan from Tencent, MiMo from Xiaomi, MiniMax, and Qwen (Tongyi Qianwen) from Alibaba Cloud. The category's defining trait is openness. Where the leading US labs keep their strongest models closed and API-only, several of these companies release full open-weight versions anyone can download, fine-tune, and run on their own infrastructure, often at a fraction of the cost of comparable Western models. Alibaba's Qwen has leaned hardest into this strategy and has been reported as the most downloaded open-weight model family globally, ahead of offerings from Meta and Google.

The real choice for a buyer isn't mainly about raw capability, since benchmark scores across the top Chinese and US models have converged and both sides now publish competitive claims. It's about governance. Using a Chinese model, whether through an API or by self-hosting open weights, raises questions about where data is processed, what the model was trained to say or avoid saying, and how it fits US and allied export-control and procurement rules. That's why every entry in this category carries a cross-border data review flag on this site.

The past year reshaped how this category is perceived. DeepSeek's early-2025 release showed a Chinese lab could match frontier performance at a much lower training cost, and it triggered a wave of price cuts and open releases across Doubao, GLM, Hunyuan, and MiniMax as competitors raced to answer it. Enterprises now treat this category less as a curiosity and more as a real, cheaper alternative, provided compliance teams sign off first.

categories.name: Data & Analytics AI
categories.blurb:
Data and analytics AI falls into two camps. One embeds AI directly into the data platform a company already uses, Snowflake Cortex, Databricks AI, Dataiku, and Tableau's Einstein features (part of Salesforce) let users ask questions in plain language and get charts, summaries, or models back without writing SQL or code. The other is built for higher-stakes operational decisions, where Palantir AIP is the clearest example, aiming to let an organization not just query data but act on it, chaining AI reasoning into workflows that touch real operations in government and enterprise settings.

The trade-off buyers actually face is governance. Once a natural-language interface can pull from any connected data source, the question of who can see what, and whether an answer can be traced back to its source data, becomes the deciding factor rather than which tool has the flashiest chat interface. Alteryx AI and Dataiku lean on this by keeping data lineage and workflow control visible as they add AI assistance, while platforms with broader natural-language reach need equally broad access controls to avoid AI surfacing data outside a user's permissions.

In the last year, text-to-SQL and natural-language BI features have become close to standard across major platforms rather than a differentiator. Databricks pushed its open DBRX model alongside a stronger governance push through Unity Catalog, aimed at giving enterprises a single control layer as more AI tools touch the same data. Notably, Databricks and Palantir also announced a strategic partnership to integrate their platforms, a sign that the space is not purely a rivalry between embedded-AI platforms and decision platforms, but increasingly one of integration between them. Palantir's AIP business has kept expanding across both commercial and government customers, reinforcing its position as the reference point for AI platforms meant to drive action, not just analysis.

categories.name: Education & Research AI
categories.blurb:
This category actually contains two different products aimed at opposite ends of the same problem. CheggMate, Grammarly for Education, and Khanmigo help students learn, write, and study, while Turnitin AI Detection exists to catch and flag AI-generated writing submitted as a student's own work. A school or district shopping here has to decide which side of that line it needs, and increasingly buys for both, which means working through FERPA and COPPA data-handling requirements for any tool touching K-12 or student records, since these products see grades, drafts, and sometimes minors' writing directly.

The past year has been rough for the "help students" side of the market and complicated for the "catch students" side. Chegg's business has continued to erode as students turn to free AI chatbots instead of paying for homework help, with reporting showing steep declines in web traffic and continued workforce cuts as the company tries to reposition around AI-assisted study tools like CheggMate rather than its older paid-answer model. Turnitin's AI detection scores remain contested, with ongoing reports of false positives flagging legitimate student writing as AI-generated, pushing some schools to treat the scores as one input rather than proof of misconduct. Khan Academy has moved the opposite direction, expanding free access to Khanmigo for more school districts and states, betting that broad, low-cost distribution matters more than per-seat revenue. Grammarly for Education sits in between, positioned as a writing-support tool rather than a detector, which keeps it out of the more adversarial part of this category.

categories.name: Enterprise AI Platforms & Agent Orchestration
categories.blurb:
Agent orchestration is the layer above a single chatbot, a platform that coordinates multiple AI agents across a company's actual systems, hands off between them, and keeps a record of what those agents did and why. That last part is what makes this a distinct buying category rather than just another chatbot purchase. Enterprises evaluating Aisera, Cognigy, Decagon, Glean, Kore.ai, Moveworks, Sierra, and Vellum aren't only asking whether the AI answers well, they're asking about role based access control, audit logs, and guardrails that keep an agent from taking an action it shouldn't. The category splits along who the agent serves. Decagon, Sierra, and Cognigy build for customer facing support, resolving tickets and conversations for a company's own customers. Moveworks, Glean, and Aisera build for employee facing use, helping staff find internal information or get IT and HR issues resolved, while Kore.ai and Vellum sit more in the platform and tooling layer that other teams build agents on top of.

This is one of the fastest moving corners of enterprise AI, and the past year showed it. Customer facing AI support agents went from pilot to real production adoption at large enterprises through 2025 and into 2026, and funding followed, Decagon reached a valuation above four billion dollars and Glean raised a new round putting its valuation above seven billion dollars as its revenue kept climbing. The employee facing side consolidated instead of just raising money, ServiceNow's acquisition of Moveworks folded one of the category's best known independent players into a larger incumbent platform, a sign that the line between standalone agent orchestration vendors and the big enterprise software suites is starting to blur. Across both sides, buyers are asking harder questions about governance dashboards and audit trails now that these agents are being trusted with more autonomy, not less.

categories.name: ERP & Business Application AI
categories.blurb:
ERP and business application AI is not a market of scrappy startups. It is the incumbent vendors retrofitting AI onto the systems companies already run finance, HR, and service operations on. Buyers here aren't shopping in an open market so much as deciding how deep to go with AI inside a platform they already pay for. Oracle Fusion AI, SAP Joule, ServiceNow Now Assist, and Workday AI each start from a different data foundation, and that shapes what they're actually good at. SAP's pitch centers on Joule Studio, a tool for building and governing custom agents on top of SAP's business processes and data model. Oracle leans on its database layer, pairing Fusion applications with an autonomous, self tuning database that it argues gives its agents a cleaner data foundation than rivals bolting AI onto older schemas. ServiceNow's strength is workflow, its agents are built to resolve IT and HR service tickets end to end rather than just summarize them. Workday's advantage is the depth of clean HR and financial data it already holds, which its Illuminate agents draw on for things like flagging finance anomalies or surfacing pay recommendations.

The real trade-off buyers weigh is scope versus control. A narrow, well governed agent that only answers questions is safe but limited, while one empowered to actually post a journal entry, approve a requisition, or change an HR record saves real labor but introduces new risk. That's exactly the shift the category made over the past year. All four vendors moved from copilot style assistants that draft and suggest toward agents with permission to take actions inside the system of record, which has raised new concern among auditors and finance leaders about erroneous or unauthorized ledger and record changes made autonomously, pushing vendors to add approval workflows, audit trails, and guardrails alongside the new autonomy.

categories.name: Finance & Legal AI
categories.blurb:
Finance and legal AI groups tools that help professionals in high-stakes, document-heavy fields find information faster and draft with more confidence, but the category splits cleanly along the two professions it serves. On the finance side, AlphaSense and Bloomberg GPT are built for market research and financial intelligence, helping analysts search earnings calls, filings, and news to surface signals faster than manual research allows. On the legal side, Harvey and CoCounsel, the latter originally built by Casetext and now owned by Thomson Reuters, handle legal research, drafting, and document review, while Kira Systems, now part of Litera, specializes narrowly in contract analysis, extracting clauses and flagging risk across large contract sets. Vanta sits adjacent to both, automating compliance evidence collection for frameworks like SOC 2, which matters to finance and legal teams managing vendor and regulatory risk.

The trade-offs buyers weigh are confidentiality and accuracy above all else. Legal tools must protect attorney-client privilege and avoid exposing work product, financial tools must guard against leaking material nonpublic information, and both fields have zero tolerance for confidently wrong answers presented as fact. That risk became concrete over the past year as courts continued sanctioning lawyers for filings containing fabricated or misquoted AI-generated citations, a problem serious enough that firms using these tools now build in mandatory citation verification steps. At the same time, adoption kept accelerating, major law firms expanded Harvey and CoCounsel deployments firm-wide, and Thomson Reuters relaunched CoCounsel as a broader agentic legal AI ecosystem in 2026, reflecting how quickly these tools moved from pilot projects to standard practice at large firms.

categories.name: Healthcare & Life Sciences AI
categories.blurb:
Healthcare and life sciences AI covers everything from decision support built into hospital software to models that design new drug molecules, and buyers in this category are choosing between fundamentally different jobs rather than competing products. Epic AI sits inside the electronic health record system most large US hospitals already run, offering tools like SlicerDicer for ad hoc data exploration and embedded AI features clinicians use without leaving their existing workflow. Google's Med-PaLM and its successor MedLM take a different approach, offering general medical reasoning and question-answering as a foundation model that health systems and software vendors build on top of. Then there are the specialists, Insilico Medicine applies AI to drug discovery and molecule design, Tempus AI focuses on precision medicine and genomics to guide oncology treatment decisions, and Merative, the former IBM Watson Health business, sells data and AI products to payers and providers.

The real trade-off is integration versus capability. A tool embedded in Epic reaches clinicians instantly but is constrained by what Epic exposes, while a standalone platform can go deeper but requires its own integration and validation work. This category also carries real regulatory weight, tools that touch diagnosis or treatment can qualify as Software as a Medical Device, subject to FDA clearance, and everything touching patient data must meet HIPAA requirements. The last year brought a steady stream of FDA clearances for AI and machine learning based devices, including the agency's first authorization of a patient-facing large language model as a medical device. Insilico Medicine advanced an AI-designed drug into Phase III trials, and Tempus AI continued expanding as a public company built around its genomic and clinical data library.

categories.name: HR & Talent AI
categories.blurb:
HR and talent AI splits into two buying motions that get lumped together but solve different problems. One side is talent intelligence and sourcing, tools like Beamery, Eightfold AI, and LinkedIn Recruiter AI that mine internal and external talent data to find and rank candidates or employees for a role. The other side is screening and interviewing, tools like HireVue and Paradox's Olivia that engage candidates directly through video assessment, chat, or scheduling. Buyers choosing a sourcing tool are mostly weighing data coverage and how well the system surfaces internal mobility candidates, not just outside hires. Buyers choosing a screening tool are weighing something else, how much of the process to automate, and how exposed that automation leaves them to bias claims and regulatory scrutiny.

That exposure runs through the whole category. HireVue's own history is the cautionary tale. It dropped facial expression analysis from its assessments after complaints and an outside audit found little evidence the visual signals it scored actually predicted job performance, and it shifted its product toward structured, job related interview questions instead. That history still shapes how buyers evaluate any AI screening tool today. The regulatory backdrop has gotten more serious over the past year. New York City's Local Law 144 keeps drawing scrutiny, a state comptroller audit and outside legal reviews found enforcement weaker than intended, but that has if anything increased pressure on vendors and employers to document bias audits and disclosures rather than relax, and other states are following with their own automated hiring rules. Meanwhile conversational recruiting agents like Paradox's Olivia have kept growing, handling scheduling and screening chat at high volume, partly because that lower stakes automation draws less regulatory heat than automated scoring or rejection decisions.

categories.name: Open Source & Self-Hosted Models
categories.blurb:
Open source and self-hosted AI is the alternative to calling a vendor's API, organizations run the model themselves, on their own hardware or cloud instance, so training data and inference traffic never leave infrastructure they control. The category splits into two layers. Frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow with Keras are for building and training models, and PyTorch has become the dominant choice for research and most new model development, with TensorFlow now mostly seen in older or production-hardened deployments. The second layer is inference and serving, where the tools differ by use case, Ollama and llama.cpp are built for running models locally on a laptop or single machine with minimal setup, while vLLM is designed for high-throughput production serving, handling many concurrent requests efficiently on server-grade GPUs. Hugging Face Transformers sits across both layers as the library most people use to load, fine-tune, and share models in the first place.

The real trade-off buyers face is engineering overhead against control. Self-hosting means owning your own uptime, scaling, and security, and it also means verifying the provenance of the model file itself, since a corrupted, mismatched, or tampered checkpoint is a genuine risk, which is why practices like maintaining an AI bill of materials for model supply chains have gained attention. The past year made self-hosting more practical than before, driven by strong open-weight model families like Llama and Qwen closing much of the capability gap with closed models. vLLM has continued to emerge as something close to a default serving engine for teams running open models at scale, and Ollama has remained the easiest on-ramp for individuals and small teams experimenting locally before committing to production infrastructure.

categories.name: Security & Identity AI
categories.blurb:
AI security tools now do more than flag suspicious activity for a human to review. The shift underway is toward autonomous detection paired with autonomous response, where the software itself isolates a compromised endpoint, revokes a session, or blocks a network connection without waiting for an analyst to click approve. That is the real change buyers are weighing, faster containment cuts damage during an active breach, but it also means a false positive or a manipulated model can lock out a legitimate user or shut down a production system on its own. This is why kill-switch controls, approval thresholds, and audit trails for automated actions have become selling points rather than afterthoughts, especially for tools with high-privilege access.

Buyers generally choose based on where they want the AI sitting. Endpoint-first platforms like SentinelOne (Purple AI) and CrowdStrike (Charlotte AI) focus on device-level detection and response. Network-layer tools such as Palo Alto Networks (Precision AI) and Zscaler apply AI to traffic inspection and access policy across a distributed workforce. Okta AI addresses identity, using behavioral signals to catch account takeover and unusual login patterns before credentials are misused. Darktrace takes an anomaly-detection-first approach, building a model of normal network behavior and flagging deviation, useful for catching threats that do not match a known signature.

The past year has seen the arms race intensify as attackers themselves use AI to write malware and craft phishing at scale, pushing vendors to compete on response speed. SentinelOne opened Purple AI's agentic investigation features more broadly to its customer base, and enterprise buyers are increasingly asking for explainability, wanting a clear record of what an AI agent did and why, not just a resolved ticket. There is also continued consolidation, with vendors bundling detection, response, and identity signals into a single AI-native platform rather than selling point tools that must be stitched together.

categories.name: Slides & Presentations
categories.blurb:
Text-to-deck generation is the shared promise across this category. Tools like Beautiful.ai, Decktopus, Gamma, Pitch AI, Presentations.AI, SlidesAI, and Tome all let a user type a topic or paste an outline and get a formatted slide deck back in minutes, with the software handling layout, image selection, and visual hierarchy instead of a person dragging text boxes around.

What actually separates them comes down to a handful of practical factors. Template and design quality varies, with some tools leaning toward polished marketing-style decks and others aimed at plain business content. Brand-kit support, locking in a company's fonts, colors, and logo, matters for teams that need every deck to look consistent without manual cleanup. Export fidelity is a recurring pain point, since a deck generated in these tools doesn't always translate cleanly into PowerPoint or Keynote for further editing. Collaboration features like comments, shared editing, and version history separate tools built for teams from tools built for solo use, and pricing splits the field between free tiers with capped exports and subscription plans aimed at business customers.

The past year brought pressure from two directions. Gamma pulled ahead as the category's breakout name, reportedly crossing $100 million in annual revenue and raising at a valuation north of $2 billion while marketing itself directly as a PowerPoint replacement. At the same time, Microsoft and Google have been building AI deck generation straight into PowerPoint and Google Slides through Copilot and Gemini, raising the bar for standalone tools to justify a separate subscription when similar generation features now come bundled into software most people already own.
